newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Cocoa, up 5 pct, is latest commodity to rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cocoa, up 5 pct, is latest commodity to rally.

text.p: Cocoa prices extended a rally on Tuesday gaining almost five percent in value as the market reacted to prospects that the Ivory Coast crop may be lower than had been expected.
London May cocoa futures hit a new five-month high of 1,024 pounds sterling per tonne as the prospect of a smaller Ivorian harvest continued to spur short-covering.
The benchmark May contract later eased slightly to close at 1,010 sterling but this was still up 29 sterling from Monday.

Ivorian Commodities Minister Alain Gauze told a meeting of the International Cocoa Organisation on Monday the country's 1996/97 crop would be less than one million tonnes, and with 800,000 already sold, there was no more to sell.
He added that the Ivory Coast, the biggest producer, planned to destroy all cocoa planted illegally in national forests, which amounted to about 100,000 tonnes last year.

"Fundamentally, production will be smaller this year and stocks will decline," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka, adding: "There will be no shortage but there will be less cocoa available this year."
Base metals lacked direction on Tuesday, while other commodities were outshined by the continued bull run in cocoa and a dramatic see-saw in coffee prices.
Inconclusive stocks data from the London Metal Exchange (LME) sent industrial metals spiralling down, but they later clawed their way up from the day's lows to end mixed.

Copper ended down $16 on the day, after an expected fall of 3,000 tonnes in warehouse stocks provided only a temporary bounce to a lagging market. Short-covering later helped prod prices up from support levels to close at $2,342 per tonne.
Short-covering also coaxed aluminium higher by the close, after a smaller than expected stock fall of just under 3,000 tonnes failed to make its mark, and left prices little changed.
Three-month aluminium closed at $1,677, up $20 from Monday's weak close of $1,657.
"Frankly the complex as a whole is looking a bit tired and needs to regroup," said one metals trader.
London robusta coffee futures ended $51 up, but well off intraday highs.
A surge in New York arabica futures on Monday sent London racing to a new nine-month peak at Tuesday's open, but keen selling saw May benchmark robusta pull back to close at $1,768.
Traders said volume was thin with many players wary of the volatility in New York.

Wild fluctuations occurred there after Monday's rally, which was inspired by a retail price hike by U.S. roaster Folgers. A number of European roasters put up prices last week as coffee hit a new high, extending its 50 percent rise this year.
Soybean prices fell after the United States Department of Agriculture surprised the market with a higher-than-expected 1996/97 stock estimate.
Furious fund buying had driven soybeans to contract highs on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT), as dealers speculated the USDA monthly report would cut its projection for U.S. soybean ending stocks.
But Tuesday's monthly report left the ending stocks estimate unchanged at 140 million bushels and pegged the soybean crush at a record 1.42 billion bushels compared to 1.41 last year.
Some die-hard bulls would not be swayed by the news. "It may open lower, but there isn't any way the funds will let it collapse," said one CBOT trader.
Wheat estimates were unchanged in the USDA report.

London gold prices fixed up on the day at $351.95 per ounce although dealers reported little follow-through buying after an early climb. "Everybody was bearish yesterday, now they're bullish today. It's that kind of market," said one dealer.

The market had turned bearish on news that the Swiss Central Bank planned to sell some of its gold reserves to set up a fund for Holocaust victims. However, sentiment turned around on Monday after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he had heard of no such plans from other central banks.
Crude oil prices were hovering around session lows by late Tuesday afternoon on bearish supply/demand fundamentals.

April futures for North Sea Brent crude were down to $19.12 per barrel by 1730 GMT, after Friday's surge above $20. May Brent which takes over as the front contract on Monday was also down on the day.
